title: Helping Teachers Do the Very Hard Thing
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer distills his MIT conference remarks on teacher learning into one claim: curriculum is itself the most powerful vehicle for developing teachers. At Desmos the aim is an asset orientation toward student thinking, and the team found that most curricula leave no room for student brilliance, so they built their own. A curriculum that is both rich and digital makes student ideas visible to teachers and coaches, which allows professional learning to be woven into daily practice. Rather than relying only on a one-time kick-off session whose energy dissipates, Desmos sends lesson-preview emails that spiral three themes: inviting, celebrating and developing student brilliance. Meyer closes with open questions about mid-range interventions, and a short link roundup follows the remarks.
points: Supporting a shift toward an asset orientation to student thinking runs aground unless the curriculum itself leaves room for student brilliance.
A curriculum that is both rich and digital lets coaches see how teachers take up practices such as selecting and sequencing student ideas.
One-time high-intensity PD dissipates quickly, so Desmos pairs it with continuous low-intensity learning delivered in the medium teachers already live in.
Preview emails spiral the same three themes all year, tied to specific screens in the next lesson, and earn open rates marketers would envy.
quotes: At Desmos, we’re convinced by a variety of research, personal experience, and trusted testimony that the most productive change a math teacher can make is to develop an asset orientation toward their students’ thinking.

It’s also digital. Students express a lot of that brilliance in a form that’s visible to teachers and the people who support teachers, including site-based coaches and coaches at Desmos. Teachers are able to enact some sophisticated routines through the platform like selecting student ideas, sequencing them, and presenting them.

Lots of curricula is one or the other. The IM curriculum is extremely rich but print-first. Lots of digital curricula only make room for student brilliance in the form of multiple choice responses and numbers—stuff that computers often grade as correct or incorrect.

We offer teachers a large kick-off session at the start of the school year to get us lined up on some of our hopes and dreams for the year and to get us excited for the work. This session is high intensity and one-time only, and we know the energy and learning dissipates quickly.

For example, teachers are always in their email. Let’s use that as a medium for professional learning. We know what lesson a teacher taught yesterday, so we send that teacher an email previewing the next lesson through the lens of one of the three themes, which we spiral throughout the year: inviting student brilliance, celebrating it, and developing it, with pedagogical techniques attached.

We offer those ideas to teachers not in a one-off session abstracted from their daily work, but rather as close to the teacher’s practice as we can get: “On this screen, here’s a great moment to tell students, ‘Look, you can’t break mathematics.’ ” These preview emails give teachers essential and generalizable teaching strategies and give us email open rates that email marketers can only dream about.
